ozet: The Prophet's years as a young man: the Fijar wars fought in the sacred months, and the Hilf al-Fudul pact made in the house of 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an to protect those who were wronged.

b07-s01: The Prophet was growing up beside his uncle Abu Talib.

Every year, in the month of Dhu al-Qa'da, a great fair was held at 'Ukaz, south-east of Mecca, between Ta'if and Nakhla. It was the greatest fair of the Arabs; people traded there, and poets recited their finest verses.
b07-s02: Many of the fairs were held in the sacred months. The Arabs held Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, Muharram and Rajab to be sacred months.
In these months fighting and bloodshed were forbidden; wars between the tribes were halted.
b07-s03: But this ban was not always kept. Several wars broke out in the sacred months between the tribe of Kinana and neighbouring tribes.
One began when a man at 'Ukaz boasted, 'I am the noblest of the Arabs'; another began with an attack on a woman there.
Because they were fought in the sacred months, these wars are called the 'Fijar wars'. Fijar means 'departing from what is right, plunging into wrongdoing'.
b07-s04: The fourth of these wars was the fiercest. On one side were the allies Quraysh and Kinana, on the other the tribes of Qays 'Aylan.

Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, the ruler of al-Hira, had sent a caravan to 'Ukaz. 'Urwa al-Rahhal of Hawazin undertook to protect it. Barrad ibn Qays of Kinana followed him and killed him in a sacred month.
b07-s05: The news reached Quraysh while they were at 'Ukaz. The men of Quraysh left without letting Hawazin know.
When Hawazin heard, they went after them. The two sides fought until Quraysh entered the Sanctuary; in the days that followed they met many more times.
b07-s06: The commander-in-chief of Quraysh and Kinana was Harb ibn Umayya; each branch also had its own commander.

Because they were in the sacred months, Abu Talib did not agree to the sons of Hashim taking part in the war. But 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an and Harb ibn Umayya insisted: 'If the sons of Hashim do not take part, neither will we.'
In the end the sons of Hashim joined the war under the command of the Prophet's uncle, al-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.
b07-s07: His uncles took the Prophet with them too. He was a young man at the time; the reports give his age as fourteen, fifteen, seventeen or twenty.
b07-s08: The Prophet described those days like this: 'I used to hand arrows to my uncles.'
He would gather the arrows shot by the enemy and give them to his uncles. According to the view preferred in the sources, he did not fight himself.
b07-s09: At the start of the war Qays 'Aylan had the upper hand; later Quraysh and Kinana won.
b07-s10: In those years, weak people who came to Mecca from outside for pilgrimage and trade were sometimes treated unjustly.
A merchant of the Zubayd tribe of Yemen sold his goods in Mecca to al-'As ibn Wa'il, one of the notables of Quraysh. But al-'As did not pay him.
b07-s11: The merchant went to the influential men of Mecca and asked for help, but those he turned to did not help him.
The next day he climbed the hill of Abu Qubays and proclaimed what had happened to him aloud, in a poem.
b07-s12: Then the Prophet's uncle al-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib went to 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an, chief of the Banu Taym and one of the richest, oldest and most influential men of Mecca, and persuaded him to hold a meeting.
In the house of 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an the clans of Quraysh gathered: Hashim, al-Muttalib, Asad, Zuhra and Taym.
b07-s13: There they swore this oath: whoever was wronged in Mecca, whether a Meccan or someone from outside, they would all stand by him together until his right was restored.
The Prophet, then about twenty years old, also took part in this pact.

Quraysh called it Hilf al-Fudul, a name explained as 'the pact of the virtuous'. From then on, those who were wronged turned to the members of this pact, and with their help their rights were restored.
b07-s14: After he became a prophet, the Messenger of Allah spoke of this pact with praise; he said that if he were called to such a pact again he would join without hesitation, and said:
'I was present at a pact in the house of 'Abdullah ibn Jud'an; I would not wish to have red camels in exchange for it. If I were called to it in the time of Islam, I would answer the call.'
